questions.question:
Statements: All pens are inks. All inks are papers.
Conclusions: I. All pens are papers. II. Some papers are pens.
questions.solution: Pens → inks → papers, so all pens are papers (I). "All pens are papers" gives the converse "some papers are pens" (II).
questions.trick: a universal always yields its "some" converse.

questions.question:
Statements: Some cats are dogs. All dogs are rats.
Conclusions: I. Some cats are rats. II. Some rats are cats.
questions.solution: The cats that are dogs are rats → some cats are rats (I); its converse gives some rats are cats (II).

questions.question:
Statements: All books are files. No file is a folder.
Conclusions: I. No book is a folder. II. Some files are books.
questions.solution: Books are files and no file is a folder → no book is a folder (I). "All books are files" converts to "some files are books" (II).

questions.question:
Statements: Some apples are red. All red are sweet.
Conclusions: I. Some apples are sweet. II. All apples are sweet.
questions.solution: Apples that are red are sweet → some apples are sweet (I). "All apples are sweet" is not forced — non-red apples are unknown.

questions.question:
Statements: All roads are streets. Some streets are lanes.
Conclusions: I. Some roads are lanes. II. Some lanes are roads.
questions.solution: Roads are streets, but the lane-streets need not be roads → I and its converse II both fail. No definite link between the two "some/all + some" links through the shared middle.

questions.question:
Statements: All keys are locks. Some locks are chains.
Conclusions: I. Some keys are chains. II. No key is a chain.
questions.solution: Keys are locks; some locks are chains. The chain-locks may or may not be keys. Neither "some keys are chains" nor "no key is a chain" is forced (Gate 1), and they are the forced pair `Some A are B ⇄ No A is B` (Gate 2).
questions.trick: a `Some/No` complementary pair, both undecided → Either.

questions.question:
Statements: Some tables are chairs. All chairs are stools.
Conclusions: I. All tables are stools. II. Some tables are not stools.
questions.solution: Some tables are stools (via chairs) is certain, but "All tables are stools" (I) and "Some tables are not stools" (II) are each undecided and form the forced pair `All ⇄ Some-not`.
questions.trick: the `All ⇄ Some-not` family is the second Either signature.

questions.question:
Statements: No dog is a cat. All cats are pets.
Conclusions: I. Some pets are not dogs. II. No dog is a pet.
questions.solution: Cats are pets and no cat is a dog → some pets (the cats) are not dogs (I). Dogs could still be pets, so II ("no dog is a pet") is not forced.

questions.question:
Statements: Only a few phones are smart. All smart are costly.
Conclusions: I. Some phones are costly. II. Some phones are not costly.
questions.solution: "Only a few phones are smart" = some phones are smart **and** some are not. Smart phones are costly → some phones are costly (I). Non-smart phones' cost is unknown, so II is not forced.
questions.trick: decode "only a few X are Y" as "some X are Y + some X are not Y".

questions.question:
Statements: Only a few doctors are engineers. No engineer is a lawyer.
Conclusions: I. Some doctors are not lawyers. II. All doctors being lawyers is a possibility.
questions.solution: Some doctors are engineers (from "only a few") and no engineer is a lawyer → those doctors are not lawyers → I follows. Since those doctor-engineers can never be lawyers, "all doctors being lawyers" is impossible → II fails.

questions.question:
Statements: All cars are buses. All buses are trains. No train is a plane.
Conclusions: I. No car is a plane. II. Some buses are not planes.
questions.solution: Cars → buses → trains, no train is a plane → no car is a plane (I). Buses are trains and no train is a plane → some buses are not planes (II).

questions.question:
Statements: Some flowers are roses. No rose is a lily. All lilies are plants.
Conclusions: I. Some flowers are not lilies. II. Some plants are not roses.
questions.solution: Rose-flowers are not lilies → some flowers are not lilies (I). Lilies are plants and no rose is a lily → some plants (lilies) are not roses (II).

questions.question:
Statements: All fruits are green. Some green are ripe. No ripe is sour.
Conclusions: I. Some fruits are ripe. II. Some green are not sour.
questions.solution: Fruits are green, but the ripe-green need not be fruits → I ("some fruits are ripe") not forced. Ripe-green are not sour → some green are not sour (II).

questions.question:
Statements: All bags are boxes. No box is a bottle. Some bottles are cups.
Conclusions: I. Some cups are boxes. II. No cup is a box.
questions.solution: Cups that are bottles are not boxes, but other cups may be boxes. "Some cups are boxes" (I) and "No cup is a box" (II) each undecided and form the `Some ⇄ No` forced pair → Either.

questions.question:
Statements: All singers are dancers. Some dancers are actors. All actors are stars.
Conclusions: I. Some dancers are stars. II. Some singers are stars.
questions.solution: Some dancers are actors, actors are stars → some dancers are stars (I). Singers are dancers but need not be the actor-dancers → II not forced.

questions.question:
Statements: No metal is wood. All wood is hard. Some hard are soft.
Conclusions: I. Some hard are not metal. II. Some metal are soft.
questions.solution: Wood is hard and no metal is wood → those hard things are not metal → some hard are not metal (I). II ("some metal are soft") has no chain support.

questions.question:
Statements: All chalks are dusters. Some dusters are pens.
Conclusions: I. Some chalks are pens. II. No chalk is a pen.
questions.solution: Chalks are dusters; some dusters are pens. The pen-dusters may or may not be chalks. "Some chalks are pens" (I) and "No chalk is a pen" (II) each undecided, forced `Some ⇄ No` pair → Either.

questions.question:
Statements: All teachers are wise. No wise is foolish. Some foolish are clever.
Conclusions: I. No teacher is foolish. II. Some clever are not wise.
questions.solution: Teachers are wise, no wise is foolish → no teacher is foolish (I). Some foolish are clever and no wise is foolish → those clever are not wise → some clever are not wise (II).

questions.question:
Statements: Some birds are eagles. All eagles are hawks. No hawk is a crow.
Conclusions: I. Some birds are hawks. II. Some eagles are not crows.
questions.solution: Birds that are eagles are hawks → some birds are hawks (I). Eagles are hawks, no hawk is a crow → some eagles are not crows (II).

questions.question:
Statements: Only a few mangoes are yellow. No yellow is green.
Conclusions: I. Some mangoes are green. II. Some mangoes are not green.
questions.solution: Some mangoes are yellow (from "only a few"); no yellow is green → those mangoes are not green → some mangoes are not green (II). I ("some mangoes are green") is not forced.

questions.question:
Statement: A > B ≥ C = D > E
Conclusions: I. A > D. II. B ≥ E.
questions.solution: A > B ≥ C = D ⇒ A > D (I). B ≥ C = D > E ⇒ B > E, so B ≥ E holds (II).

questions.question:
Statement: P ≤ Q < R = S ≤ T
Conclusions: I. P < R. II. Q ≤ T.
questions.solution: P ≤ Q < R ⇒ P < R (I). Q < R = S ≤ T ⇒ Q < T, so Q ≤ T holds (II).

questions.question:
Statement: L > M = N ≥ O < P
Conclusions: I. L > O. II. P > M.
questions.solution: L > M = N ≥ O ⇒ L > O (I). For II, both P and M sit above O (P > O, M ≥ O) with no direct link → P > M not forced.

questions.question:
Statement: A > B ≤ C = D
Conclusions: I. A > D. II. A ≤ D.
questions.solution: A > B ≤ C = D breaks the chain at B (`> then ≤`), so A vs D is undecided. I (A > D) and II (A ≤ D) are the forced pair `> ⇄ ≤` → Either.
questions.trick: a `>` immediately followed by `≤`/`<` (opposite-facing signs) snaps the chain; if conclusions are the complementary `>`/`≤` pair, answer Either.

questions.question:
Statement: P < Q = R ≥ S
Conclusions: I. P < S. II. P ≥ S.
questions.solution: P < Q = R ≥ S: the `< then ≥` break leaves P vs S undecided. I (P < S) and II (P ≥ S) are the forced `< ⇄ ≥` pair → Either.

questions.question:
Statement: M ≥ N > O = P ≥ Q
Conclusions: I. M > P. II. N ≥ Q.
questions.solution: M ≥ N > O = P ⇒ M > P (I). N > O = P ≥ Q ⇒ N > Q, so N ≥ Q holds (II).

questions.question:
Statement: D = E ≥ F > G ≤ H
Conclusions: I. D ≥ F. II. E > G.
questions.solution: D = E ≥ F ⇒ D ≥ F (I). E ≥ F > G ⇒ E > G (II).

questions.question:
Statement: A < B = C > D ≥ E
Conclusions: I. A < D. II. B > E.
questions.solution: A < B = C > D: A and D are both below C with no link → I (A < D) not forced. B = C > D ≥ E ⇒ B > E (II).

questions.question:
Statement: A ≤ B = C ≥ D ≥ E
Conclusions: I. A < C. II. B > E.
questions.solution: A ≤ B = C ⇒ A ≤ C, so "A < C" is not guaranteed (equality possible) → I fails. B = C ≥ D ≥ E ⇒ B ≥ E, so "B > E" not guaranteed → II fails.
questions.trick: a strict conclusion (`<`,`>`) drawn from a chain containing `≥`/`≤`/`=` only is unsafe when equality can absorb the gap — that is a Neither, not an Either.

questions.question:
Statement: L > M ≥ N = O ≤ P
Conclusions: I. L > N. II. L > P.
questions.solution: L > M ≥ N ⇒ L > N (I). N = O ≤ P puts P above N; L is also above N, so L vs P undecided → II (L > P) fails.

questions.context:
In the following questions the symbols are used with these meanings:
- `A # B` → A is **not smaller than** B (A ≥ B)
- `A $ B` → A is **not greater than** B (A ≤ B)
- `A % B` → A is **neither greater than nor equal to** B (A < B)
- `A & B` → A is **neither smaller than nor equal to** B (A > B)
- `A * B` → A is **neither greater than nor smaller than** B (A = B)
questions.question:
Statements: P & Q, Q # R, R * S
Conclusions: I. P & S. II. R $ P.
questions.solution: P > Q, Q ≥ R, R = S. I: P > Q ≥ R = S ⇒ P > S = `P & S` (true). II: P > Q ≥ R ⇒ P > R ⇒ R < P ⇒ R ≤ P = `R $ P` (true).

questions.solution: P < Q, Q = R, R > S. I: S < R = Q ⇒ S < Q = `S % Q` (true). II: P < Q = R ⇒ P < R = `P % R` (true).

questions.question:
Statements: A * B, B $ C, C # D
Conclusions: I. A % C. II. A * C.
questions.solution: A = B ≤ C gives A ≤ C (proven). I: `A % C` (A < C). II: `A * C` (A = C). Since A ≤ C is established, exactly one of `<` / `=` holds → forced derived pair → Either.
questions.trick: whenever you can prove `≤` (or `≥`) and the two conclusions are the matching `<`/`=` (or `>`/`=`) split, it is Either.
